artwork.title: Lady of Auxerre
artwork.imageCredit: Photo: Shonagon, 2023, via Wikimedia Commons · CC0

lessons.title: A stranger in the museum

n1.text: She is less than a metre tall and carved in limestone. She stands very straight, feet together, one arm bent across her body.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Step close. Look at her face first, then follow her right arm across her body.

q1.text: Her style is called Daedalic. Who was Daedalus?

b1a.text: Yes. Daedalus is a figure of legend. Scholars borrowed his name for a whole 7th-century style: frontal bodies, flat faces, hair in stiff rows.

correction.truth: Daedalic is a modern name for a 7th-century style, taken from a legendary craftsman. Her maker is unknown.
correction.evidence: Fullerton, Greek Sculpture (2016); the Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus.

correction.tempting: Names borrowed from Greek myth often belong to gods.
correction.truth: Daedalus was a legendary craftsman, and scholars named the style after him.
correction.evidence: Fullerton, Greek Sculpture (2016); the Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus.

n2.text: Look at her hair: long locks, cut into layers like steps, falling over her chest. Traces of red paint survive on her bust.

q2.text: Where was she most probably made?

b2a.text: She carries the town's name, but she was not made there.

correction.tempting: She is called the Lady of Auxerre.
correction.truth: Scholars agree she was most probably made on Crete, far from France.

b2b.text: Yes. Scholars agree on Crete. Some go further and name the town of Eleutherna: its museum says the stone matches, while the Louvre still writes a question mark.

correction.tempting: She was shown in Athens in 2004 and 2005.
correction.truth: That was an exhibition loan. Scholars agree she was most probably made on Crete.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; the Eleutherna museum; Collignon (1913); Fullerton (2016).

n3.text: She was made in the 7th century BC. She probably left Crete in the late 1800s. By then she belonged to a collector named Bourgoin.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Over two thousand years old, and nobody wrote down where she was dug up.

q3.text: Why is she called the Lady of Auxerre?

choices.label: She was a lady of Auxerre

correction.tempting: The title sounds like a portrait.
correction.truth: She is named after the town where she was found. There is no inscription and no name.

b3b.text: Auxerre is in France, far from Crete.

correction.tempting: Many works are named after their maker's town.
correction.truth: Her maker is unknown, and she was most probably made on Crete. Auxerre is where she was found.

b3c.text: Yes. In 1907 an archaeologist noticed her in the museum of Auxerre, a French town, and the town's name stuck.

choices.label: The man who dug her up

n4.text: The museum in Auxerre had no record of how she arrived: the curator searched the register and the catalogue and found nothing.

b4a.text: Yes. The archaeologist Maxime Collignon noticed her in the Auxerre museum in 1907 and saw that she was a Greek work in the style of Crete.

b4b.text: He was the one who could not find her in the books.

correction.truth: A visiting archaeologist, Maxime Collignon, spotted her; the curator then searched the museum's records in vain.
correction.evidence: Collignon (1913), quoting the curator's letter; Rolley (1964).

correction.truth: No record says where or by whom she was dug up. She was already in the Auxerre museum when Collignon saw her.

n5.text: Collignon asked the national museums to act. In 1908 their director proposed talks with the town of Auxerre.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Auxerre owned her. The Louvre wanted her. How would you settle that?

q5.text: How did the Louvre get her in 1909?

correction.tempting: He found her and asked the national museums to get her.
correction.truth: She belonged to the museum of Auxerre. The Louvre swapped a painting for her.

correction.tempting: The town's museum let her go to Paris.
correction.truth: It was an exchange: Auxerre received a landscape painting by Harpignies.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record and its 1909 report; Rolley (1964); Collignon (1913).

b5c.text: Yes. Auxerre received a landscape by the painter Harpignies, and the Louvre received the statue.

n6.text: A Cretan statue of the 7th century BC, a French town museum, a swap for a painting. Today she stands in Room 170, on Floor −1 of the Denon wing.

lessons.takeaway: A small statue, most probably made on Crete in the 7th century BC, stood unrecognised in a French town museum until 1907; the Louvre swapped a painting for her.
